question: What is the primary physiological function of the integumentary system?

options.A: Acting as a protective barrier against external pathogens
options.B: Synthesizing primary red blood cells for systemic circulation
options.C: Producing primary structural enzymes for digestion
options.D: Regulating baseline endocrine hormone production in the body

explanation: The skin forms the body's first line of defense against physical, chemical, and biological invaders in the environment. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T2#GNS213_U5_T2_h1)

question: Why must nurses assess the integumentary system during a routine physical examination?

options.A: Cutaneous changes frequently indicate underlying systemic diseases
options.B: Skin conditions are always isolated and rarely affect other organs
options.C: Integumentary structures are the only organs visible to the naked eye
options.D: Dermal assessments eliminate the need for routine blood work

explanation: Many internal metabolic, circulatory, and autoimmune disorders produce visible physical manifestations on the skin, hair, and nails. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T2#GNS213_U5_T2_h1)

question: What information is essential to collect first when a client reports a new skin rash?

options.A: The brand of soap used during childhood years
options.B: The client's exact blood type and family ancestry
options.C: Previous surgical procedures unrelated to the skin
options.D: Onset, duration, and exact location of the lesion

explanation: Establishing when the skin issue started, how long it has lasted, and where it is located helps narrow down differential diagnoses. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T2#GNS213_U5_T2_h2)

question: A client taking a new medication presents with a sudden generalized rash. Why is this drug history crucial?

options.A: Many pharmaceutical agents trigger adverse cutaneous drug reactions
options.B: Medications alter the pH of sweat glands directly
options.C: All drugs block the synthesis of melanin in the epidermis
options.D: Prescription drugs permanently change baseline skin color

explanation: Adverse drug reactions commonly manifest as skin rashes, making a thorough medication history essential for identifying the offending agent. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T2#GNS213_U5_T2_h2)

question: Which lighting condition is optimal for performing a thorough physical examination of the skin?

options.A: Complete darkness supplemented by a single colored bulb
options.B: Direct ultraviolet light to stimulate melanin production
options.C: Dim yellow lighting to highlight subtle skin contours
options.D: Bright natural daylight or adequate overhead illumination

explanation: Good lighting is vital to accurately assess skin color, pallor, cyanosis, and subtle lesion borders without distortion. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T2#GNS213_U5_T2_h3)

question: When must the nurse don clean gloves during an integumentary physical assessment?

options.A: Throughout the entire duration of every routine health history interview
options.B: Only when the client has a diagnosed systemic viral illness
options.C: When palpating non-intact skin, open wounds, or moist lesions
options.D: Whenever the ambient room temperature drops below normal limits

explanation: Standard precautions require barrier protection whenever there is a risk of contact with blood, body fluids, or non-intact cutaneous surfaces. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T2#GNS213_U5_T2_h3)

question: Which clinical technique is used to evaluate skin turgor and hydration status?

options.A: Percussing the dorsal surface of both hands and forearms
options.B: Gently pinching a fold of skin and observing return time
options.C: Auscultating blood flow across prominent superficial vessels
options.D: Measuring the exact circumference of the lower extremities

explanation: Skin turgor is checked by lifting a fold of skin and noting how quickly it returns to its normal flat position. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T2#GNS213_U5_T2_h4)

question: Where should a nurse look to assess for pallor or cyanosis in a client with deeply pigmented skin?

options.A: The lateral surfaces of the calves
options.D: The dorsum of the upper thighs

explanation: Areas with less natural pigmentation, such as mucous membranes and nail beds, reveal underlying vascular color changes more clearly. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T2#GNS213_U5_T2_h4)

question: What defines a primary skin lesion classified as a macule?

options.A: A depressed crater extending deep into the subcutaneous tissue
options.B: A flat, circumscribed color change measuring less than 1 cm
options.C: A thick, firm plaque caused by chronic scratching habits
options.D: An elevated, fluid-filled blister measuring greater than 2 cm

explanation: A macule is strictly flat and non-palpable with a distinct border, such as a simple freckle or flat mole. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T2#GNS213_U5_T2_h5)

question: A client presents with an elevated skin lesion containing cloudy, purulent exudate. How should the nurse document this finding?
explanation: Lesions filled with pus, like an acne pimple or small abscess, are accurately classified as pustules. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T2#GNS213_U5_T2_h5)

question: What is the normal angle between the nail base and the nail plate in a healthy individual?
explanation: A normal nail bed angle is approximately 160 degrees; an increased angle indicates clubbing often linked to hypoxia. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T2#GNS213_U5_T2_h6)

question: Why does a nurse assess capillary refill on a client's fingernails?

options.A: To evaluate peripheral vascular perfusion and blood flow
options.B: To determine total body fat composition and hydration
options.C: To screen for localized fungal infections of the nail bed
options.D: To measure the exact concentration of serum hemoglobin

explanation: Capillary refill time reflects how efficiently the peripheral cardiovascular system circulates blood to the extremities. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T2#GNS213_U5_T2_h6)

question: Which diagnostic tool uses ultraviolet light to detect fluorescent fungal or bacterial skin infections?
explanation: A Wood's lamp emits ultraviolet light that causes specific microorganisms or pigmented areas to fluoresce in a dark room. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T2#GNS213_U5_T2_h7)

question: What is the primary clinical purpose of performing a skin biopsy on a suspicious lesion?

options.A: Measuring exact internal body temperature and metabolic rate
options.B: Instilling therapeutic antibiotics directly into deep tissues
options.C: Permanently removing the root cause of systemic allergies
options.D: Obtaining tissue samples for definitive histological examination

explanation: A biopsy removes a small piece of tissue so pathologists can examine cellular architecture under a microscope to confirm a diagnosis. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T2#GNS213_U5_T2_h7)

question: Which practice is essential when documenting integumentary findings in a client's medical record?

options.A: Omit measuring lesion dimensions to save time during busy shifts
options.B: Relying on general subjective labels like 'bad rash' or 'skin sore'
options.C: Using precise descriptive terms and exact measurements in centimeters
options.D: Recording only findings that the client specifically complains about

explanation: Clear, objective documentation with measurements ensures accurate tracking of lesion changes over time by all healthcare providers. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T2#GNS213_U5_T2_h8)

question: Why is timely reporting of a rapidly changing, irregular skin lesion critical in clinical practice?

options.A: It prevents normal physiological aging processes from occurring
options.B: It guarantees immediate discharge from the inpatient unit
options.C: It facilitates early detection of potential malignant melanoma
options.D: It eliminates the need for any further nursing assessments

explanation: Prompt identification and reporting of suspicious skin changes allow for early specialist referral and timely cancer treatment. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T2#GNS213_U5_T2_h8)
